newsitem.title: SURINAM: Alcoa Suriname unit looks to brighter future.
newsitem.headline: Alcoa Suriname unit looks to brighter future.

text.p: Aluminum Co of America's (Alcoa) Suriname unit Suralco, after surviving guerrilla warfare, unfavorable economic policies and a major dip in international prices, is looking forward to a smoother ride in coming years.
"We've had to finance everything for the last few years out of our own cash flow," Suralco President Henk Ramdin told Reuters in an interview.
"But now, if I went to them (Alcoa) for money, I'm pretty sure I'd get it. The situation has changed."
In the late 1980s everything seemed to be against the company that accounts for about 75 percent of Suriname's export earnings -- some $300 million per year.
An armed uprising against the military government in the late 1980s forced Suriname, once the world's biggest bauxite exporter, to import the raw material for its alumina plant.

Peace was restored by a democratically elected government in 1992 but weak international prices and an exchange rate system forcing Suralco to sell its product well below the parallel rate at which its costs were measured had the company on its knees.
"We weren't making any money. The investment program had come to a complete halt," Ramdin said.
A new bauxite accord signed with the government in 1993 gave Suralco access to a unified exchange rate, and international prices improved.
"We're making money now. We're paying about $2 million in income tax per month," he said. Corporate income taxes are 38 percent in Suriname.

Investment has resumed with over $150 million spent opening up new areas of existing bauxite mines in the last three years. Another $300 million has been earmarked for upgrading facilities and cutting costs.
Alumina and aluminum output will rise about 10 percent to 1.7 million tonnes and 33,000 tonnes respectively in 1997, but will not increase much beyond that for the foreseeable future.

Sixty percent of Suralco's bauxite needs come from its own mine near the Paranam alumina processing and aluminum smelter plants, 20 miles (30 km) south of Paramaribo. The remainder comes from the Billiton mine run by South Africa's General Mining Union Co at Moengo, about 55 miles (90 km) east of the capital, in which it has a minority stake
Reserves at the two mines should last until 2011, but Suralco and Billiton have three other concession areas under study.
"In the past, these areas were classified as non-commercial and non-economic but we're taking another look at them and I believe one of the three will become a mine," Ramdin said.

Large bauxite deposits are also known to exist at Bakhuys, in western Suriname. "There's between 150 and 200 million tonnes. That's four million tonnes a year for 25 years but it would require a major investment."
Suralco's other big challenge is cutting costs. Reducing the 2,200 workforce would be one obvious way. But there is a snag.
"We have technical possibilities to reduce manpower but we have to get government approval to dismiss people," Ramdin said.
Still, he estimates natural wastage means about 100 employees retire or leave each year. "The ideal would be to cut it to about 1,800 over two to three years."
A bitter wage dispute closed Suralco down for about three weeks last June. But with inflation low and a generous settlement paid last year, Radmin expects fewer problems this year.
As Suriname's biggest exporter earner, a lot is expected of Suralco by the government and the people. "It is always a pressure. It's a tremenous responsibility we carry," Ramdin said.
((-- Caracas newsroom, 582 505 2600))
